paragraphs: Scientific observations often combine several sources that researchers want to study separately. Overlapping galaxies are one example: the recorded image contains blended contributions rather than a clean picture of each galaxy. This paper develops a diffusion-model approach to separating such sources without explicitly specifying a simplified model of what each source should look like.

The central requirement is access to multiple views, where different observations contain different linear transformations of the unknown sources. These views provide complementary information about the mixture. The method learns source distributions even when no source is observed alone, and the observations contain noise, missing information, or different resolutions.

The learned models support more than a single proposed separation. They can generate samples from source distributions, assess candidate sources, and sample joint source explanations conditioned on an observation. This makes uncertainty part of the reconstruction process. Demonstrations on synthetic problems and real galaxy observations support the approach, showing how multiple views can replace explicit source assumptions with distributions learned from data.
neurips-2025-a-data-driven-prism-multi-v.tldr: Diffusion models learn to separate mixed sources from multiple observation views, including noisy and incomplete data.

paragraphs: An agent can store past experiences without organizing them in a way that helps with future tasks. A-Mem addresses this distinction by letting an agent dynamically organize its memory. The motivation is that fixed storage operations and structures can restrict how well a memory system adapts to different tasks and contexts.

The system draws on Zettelkasten, an approach built around interconnected notes. Each new memory becomes a structured note with contextual descriptions, keywords, and tags. A-Mem examines earlier memories and adds connections where meaningful similarities exist. The resulting network organizes experiences through relationships as well as through the attributes attached to individual notes.

New experiences can also change existing memories: their contextual representations and attributes may be updated as related information arrives. Memory therefore evolves instead of merely accumulating entries. Experiments involving six foundation models report improvements over existing leading baselines. These results support the usefulness of combining structured notes with agent-directed linking and revision for more adaptive memory management.
neurips-2025-a-mem-agentic-memory-for-ll.tldr: A-Mem gives agents an evolving network of linked memories whose organization and descriptions can change as new experiences arrive.

paragraphs: Encouraging language models to produce extended reasoning often involves expensive training. This paper investigates whether internal activity can instead be adjusted directly. It identifies a small set of influential activations in the final layers that strongly affect properties such as response length and self-reflection. Amplifying these activations and adding “wait” tokens elicits longer reasoning without training.

The authors also observe a recurring pattern: these activations rise sharply after special tokens and then decay exponentially. Their general control method uses a few contrasting examples to locate the relevant activations, then applies simple mathematical functions to adjust them during generation. This turns an observed internal pattern into a practical inference-time intervention.

Experiments report increased self-reflection and improved reasoning performance from these controls. The paper also introduces a separate, parameter-efficient training method that updates an activation amplification module in the last layer and a few LoRA layers. That method outperforms LoRA on reasoning benchmarks while training substantially fewer parameters, suggesting that targeted changes to late-layer activity can be useful both with and without fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-activation-control-for-effi.tldr: Targeted control of late-layer activations elicits extended reasoning without training and also supports more parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Generalized additive models combine component contributions in a structure that is often considered understandable. That reputation raises a separate computational question: can meaningful explanations always be obtained efficiently? This paper investigates the computational difficulty of producing different explanations for several forms of additive models, rather than treating structural interpretability as an assurance of easy explanation.

The analysis finds that the answer depends strongly on the allowed input space. Component model choices also matter, but their effects emerge only in particular input domains. Regression and classification introduce further differences. Together, these findings show why an explanation method that is feasible in one additive-model setting may become computationally difficult in another.

Under standard complexity assumptions, including P not equaling NP, the paper establishes both tractable and hard cases. It also finds that expressing complex models such as neural networks additively can simplify explanation, but only for certain explanation methods and domains. The contribution is a conditional map of feasibility: understanding the model's structure is only part of determining whether a requested explanation can be computed efficiently.
neurips-2025-additive-models-explained-a.tldr: Explaining additive models can be computationally easy or hard depending on the input domain, component models, task, and explanation method.

paragraphs: Classification becomes difficult when observations are noisy or categories overlap. This paper proposes an adaptive quantum circuit for combining uncertain evidence using Dempster's rule. The circuit operates within quantum evidence theory, which supports decisions based on both basic probability and plausibility. Its purpose is to make evidence combination more computationally efficient while retaining the classical fusion result.

The authors report a deterministic computation whose quantum fusion outcomes exactly match those of the classical method. They also claim an exponential reduction in the computational complexity of evidence combination. The speed claim concerns this combination operation, connecting a familiar uncertainty-reasoning rule to a quantum implementation that preserves its output.

A further contribution explains how quantities in quantum evidence theory correspond to circuit representations and measurements. The basic probability amplitude function supplies amplitude encoding, while basic probability distributions and plausibility functions represent measurement outcomes for their respective decision levels. These connections give the proposed circuit an interpretation in terms of uncertain evidence, alongside its claimed computational advantage for classification.
neurips-2025-an-adaptive-quantum-circuit.tldr: An adaptive quantum circuit implements Dempster's evidence-combination rule with matching classical outcomes and a claimed exponential reduction in combination complexity.

paragraphs: Multi-agent workflows often represent a task as a graph of dependent subtasks. This structure assumes that parent responses provide enough context to make other subtasks conditionally independent, and that their outputs are reliable. The paper argues that these assumptions frequently break during execution, producing inconsistencies and coordination failures when correct answers are unavailable for direct checking.

SeqCV responds by executing subtasks sequentially and conditioning each one on all previously verified responses. It checks consistency after short stretches of generated text. A stretch is accepted only when diverse language models consistently support it as shared knowledge. Otherwise, the system discards it and recursively divides the subtask into smaller reasoning steps.

The intended benefit is to catch misalignment before it propagates through the workflow. Although execution is sequential, the authors report higher effective throughput than parallel pipelines because SeqCV avoids repeatedly correcting the same inconsistency. Across the evaluated reasoning and coordination tasks, accuracy improves by up to 30% over existing agent systems. The findings connect productive throughput to the amount of corrective work, not simply the amount of parallel execution.
neurips-2025-can-dependencies-induced-by.tldr: SeqCV uses sequential execution and frequent cross-model consistency checks to reduce coordination failures in multi-agent reasoning.

paragraphs: Interpreting genes and genetic variants requires researchers to extract and weigh evidence from scientific publications. CGBench evaluates language models on this work using expert-curated interpretations from ClinGen. Its aim is to move beyond narrow scientific-data tasks toward the detailed literature interpretation involved in clinical genetics research.

The benchmark separates several abilities: extracting experimental results according to precise guidelines, assessing evidence strength, and categorizing and describing experimental outcomes. Testing eight language models reveals substantial gaps, particularly in following fine-grained instructions. Reasoning models perform better on detailed tasks, while models without that designation perform better on higher-level interpretation in the reported evaluation.

The authors also compare model explanations with human explanations using a language-model judge. This reveals a consequential distinction: a model can assign the correct evidence category while hallucinating or misinterpreting the supporting results. The benchmark therefore examines both decisions and their explanations. Its findings suggest that success on a classification score alone can obscure weaknesses in the scientific interpretation that is supposed to justify the answer.
neurips-2025-cgbench-benchmarking-langua.tldr: CGBench finds that correct evidence classifications can conceal flawed scientific explanations in language models interpreting clinical genetics literature.

paragraphs: This paper studies theoretical constraints on how Transformers learn sequences. It identifies two phenomena, isolation and continuity, that can interfere with learning even simple patterns. The mathematical claims apply to Transformers that use compact positional encoding, making that architectural condition central to the scope of the results.

Isolation means that a learnable sequence must be separated from another learnable sequence. As a consequence, some sequences cannot both be learned by the same Transformer. Continuity describes a different effect: a learned sequence develops an attractor basin around it. Sequences that fall within this basin collapse toward the learned sequence rather than remaining distinct.

Together, these phenomena concern the ability to preserve distinctions between patterns while learning them. The authors prove that both arise under the stated positional-encoding condition and design experiments showing that the limitations also appear at practical scales. The contribution combines a formal explanation of sequence-learning difficulties with empirical demonstrations that the effects are relevant beyond the mathematical analysis.
neurips-2025-continuity-and-isolation-le.tldr: For Transformers with compact positional encoding, the paper proves two phenomena that restrict learning and distinguishing certain sequences.

paragraphs: Multimodal models often train with every input modality present, but deployment can provide only a changing subset. CyIN addresses the resulting mismatch by training one model to handle both complete and incomplete inputs. Its approach combines task-focused internal representations with reconstruction of information from missing modalities.

First, CyIN cyclically applies information bottlenecks across modalities at the token and label levels. These bottlenecks use variational approximation to retain task-related features while reducing information that is less useful for the task. The resulting latent representations are intended to make interactions between modalities and their eventual combination more efficient.

Second, cross-modal cyclic translation reconstructs missing modalities from those that remain, using forward and reverse processes. The model combines the extracted and reconstructed informative representations in a shared learning framework. Experiments on four multimodal datasets report superior performance with both complete inputs and diverse missing-modality settings. The findings support treating missing inputs within the same learning process used for fully observed examples, with reconstruction supplying information that would otherwise be absent.
neurips-2025-cyin-cyclic-informative-lat.tldr: CyIN combines information bottlenecks and cyclic reconstruction to train a single multimodal model for complete and missing-input settings.

paragraphs: Training on extended reasoning examples can teach a model useful reasoning behavior while also encouraging it to absorb problem-specific shortcuts. The authors find that ordinary supervised fine-tuning on such examples can reduce performance outside the training distribution. DLoFT targets this problem by changing which part of the training signal updates the model.

The method separates the gradient into two orthogonal components: one associated with the general long-reasoning paradigm and another associated with specific problem content. It uses the response's thinking and solution phases to identify the content-related direction through projection. Orthogonalization then separates out the component intended to capture the broader reasoning pattern, and only that component updates model parameters.

This mechanism aims to teach the form of systematic reasoning while reducing memorization of the particular knowledge and heuristics in training examples. Experiments report significantly better generalization than supervised fine-tuning while maintaining strong performance on problems from the training distribution. The result supports the value of selecting training directions, rather than using the full gradient from every reasoning example.
neurips-2025-dloft-gradient-decoupled-fi.tldr: DLoFT separates training gradients to emphasize general long-form reasoning behavior and improve generalization beyond training problems.

paragraphs: CLIP classifies images by relating their representations to text representations, yet the two can lie far apart in its feature space. This paper finds that adversarial perturbations amplify that mismatch and damage classification. COLA addresses the mismatch directly through a training-free alignment procedure that can also work with already fine-tuned models.

The procedure first projects an adversarial image representation into the space spanned by class text features. This is designed to remove distortions unrelated to meaning while retaining information that distinguishes classes. It then treats multiple augmented image and text views as distributions and uses optimal transport to refine their alignment, incorporating the projection into the matching cost.

These steps address both overall image-text alignment and local structure among representations. Evaluation across 14 zero-shot classification benchmarks supports the method's effectiveness. On ImageNet and its variants, the authors report an average improvement of 6.7% under PGD adversarial attacks while retaining high accuracy on clean inputs. The findings show that adjusting cross-modal relationships can improve robustness without an additional training stage.
neurips-2025-enhancing-clip-robustness-v.tldr: COLA improves CLIP's adversarial robustness without training by projecting and realigning image and text representations.

paragraphs: Testing a new model architecture usually requires costly pretraining before its quality becomes clear. This paper introduces grafting: editing a pretrained diffusion Transformer to explore alternative designs with a small additional compute budget. An analysis of activations and attention locality guides a testbed built around DiT-XL/2.

The authors replace attention with gated convolution, local attention, or linear attention, and modify the model's feed-forward components. Many resulting hybrids achieve FID scores of 2.38–2.64, compared with 2.27 for the original model, using less than 2% of its pretraining compute. This provides a way to investigate architectural choices while retaining much of a pretrained model's quality.

The experiments also extend beyond individual component replacements. Grafting PixArt-Σ produces a 1.43× speedup with less than a 2% reduction in GenEval score. Another edit converts pairs of sequential blocks into parallel blocks, halving depth and achieving better quality than other models of comparable depth. Together, these cases show that pretrained models can support exploration of both alternative operators and broader architectural restructuring.
neurips-2025-exploring-diffusion-transfo.tldr: Grafting edits pretrained diffusion Transformers to test new components and architectures at a small fraction of pretraining cost.

paragraphs: Spatial questions can require a vision-language model to connect precise visual observations with several reasoning steps. SpatialReasoner-R1 targets weaknesses in that combination. The paper develops both a method for generating detailed reasoning supervision and a training objective that distinguishes different parts of a response.

Its Multi-Model Monte Carlo Tree Search generates diverse, logically consistent long reasoning trajectories. Fine-grained Direct Preference Optimization then applies segment-specific preferences to descriptive grounding and logical reasoning. A spatial reward evaluates visual consistency, spatial grounding, and logical coherence, allowing the training signal to reflect these different requirements within an answer.

Compared with standard preference optimization, the fine-grained method delivers relative gains of 4.1% on spatial quality tasks and 9.0% on spatial quantity tasks. The resulting model sets a new best result on SpatialRGPT-Bench, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.8% in average accuracy, while remaining competitive on general vision-language tasks. These findings support supervising the distinct descriptive and reasoning portions of spatial responses rather than treating their quality as a single undifferentiated judgment.
neurips-2025-fine-grained-preference-opt.tldr: SpatialReasoner-R1 improves spatial reasoning through searched reasoning examples and preference training that separately evaluates descriptive and logical segments.

paragraphs: Shuffled regression asks how to learn a relationship when the inputs and outputs are available but their pairings are unknown. Gaussian Process Shuffled Regression addresses both the unknown function and the missing correspondence probabilistically. A Gaussian process prior, specified through a kernel, allows flexible functions and supplies uncertainty estimates for predictions.

The authors connect their model's marginal likelihood and predictive distribution to those of ordinary Gaussian process regression. Using Bayesian evidence maximization, they derive an iterative algorithm that alternates between applying standard regression and updating the input-output correspondence. This connection makes familiar Gaussian process machinery useful in a setting where the training pairs themselves must be inferred.

For lower computational cost, the paper also develops a sparse approximation in weight space. This version can be understood as Bayesian shuffled linear regression using random Fourier features, and it permits closed-form correspondence updates. Benchmark experiments support the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The contribution combines flexible regression, prediction uncertainty, and correspondence estimation within one model, alongside a more computationally economical variant.
neurips-2025-gaussian-processes-for-shuf.tldr: GPSR learns flexible regression functions and prediction uncertainty when the pairing between inputs and outputs is unknown.

paragraphs: Predicting where an image was taken requires distinguishing visually plausible places across the world. Many approaches first retrieve candidate locations and then select a match. GeoRanker focuses on this selection stage, where simple similarity scores and separate judgments of individual candidates can miss geographic relationships between the options.

The framework uses a large vision-language model to jointly represent interactions between the query image and its candidates and predict geographic proximity. Its multi-order distance loss trains the model to rank both absolute and relative distances. This makes structured spatial relationships part of the learning objective, rather than relying only on whether a candidate looks similar.

The authors also introduce GeoRanking, a dataset designed specifically for geographic ranking with multimodal candidate information. GeoRanker achieves state-of-the-art results on IM2GPS3K and YFCC4K, significantly outperforming the strongest existing methods in those evaluations. The results support treating candidate selection as a geographic ranking problem, with supervision that captures how the possible locations relate spatially to the query and to one another.
neurips-2025-georanker-distance-aware-ra.tldr: GeoRanker improves image geolocation by learning to rank candidate locations using absolute and relative geographic distances.

paragraphs: Agents in a language-model team often process overlapping conversation content repeatedly. Ordinary key-value caching cannot simply eliminate this work because each agent may place that content after a different prefix, changing the cached representations. KVCOMM targets these differences so that shared content can be reused across agents without training.

The method maintains a pool of cached examples called anchors. These record how cache values differ under varying prefixes. KVCOMM consults them to estimate and adjust the caches for shared content, aligning their offsets with the receiving agent's context. Updating the anchor pool online allows adaptation to changing requests and context structures.

Across evaluated retrieval, mathematics, and collaborative coding workloads, the framework reports more than 70% cache reuse without quality degradation. In a fully connected five-agent setup with 1K input tokens per agent, including 512 prefix tokens, and 512 output tokens, it achieves up to a 7.8× speedup over standard prefilling. Time to first token falls from roughly 430 to 55 milliseconds. This demonstrates substantial savings in the context-processing stage under the stated configuration.
neurips-2025-kvcomm-online-cross-context.tldr: KVCOMM reuses shared-content caches across agents by adjusting for different prefixes, reducing repeated context processing without training.

paragraphs: A benchmark score is useful only insofar as it measures the capability or property it is meant to represent. This paper examines that connection through construct validity: whether an evaluation captures what matters to a complex concept such as safety or robustness. The concern is especially relevant when benchmark results inform judgments before deployment.

A team of 29 expert reviewers systematically reviews 445 language-model benchmarks from leading natural language processing and machine learning conferences. They identify recurring patterns involving the phenomena being measured, the tasks chosen to represent them, and the metrics used to score performance. These patterns undermine the validity of claims made from the resulting evaluations.

The paper responds with eight recommendations and detailed practical guidance for benchmark developers and users. Its contribution is to connect evaluation design with the strength of the conclusions an evaluation can support. A task and a scoring rule do more than produce a number: their relationship to the intended concept determines how that number should be interpreted.
neurips-2025-measuring-what-matters-cons.tldr: A review of 445 language-model benchmarks finds validity problems in how concepts, tasks, and scores support evaluation claims.

paragraphs: Longer contexts make conventional attention increasingly expensive because its computational cost grows quadratically with sequence length. MoBA addresses this burden by applying mixture-of-experts principles to attention. The goal is to let the model determine where to attend while reducing the need to process every possible attention connection.

The design follows a preference for less predefined structure. Instead of fixing attention around particular windows or other task-specific patterns, it gives the model control over attention selection. A central feature is the ability to move between full and sparse attention. This flexibility allows the architecture to support different levels of attention computation within the same approach.

The authors report superior performance on long-context tasks alongside efficient attention computation, and state that MoBA has already been used for production workloads requiring long contexts. The contribution therefore concerns both architecture and practical use. Its stated findings support learned attention selection as a way to make long-context processing more efficient while preserving the ability to use full attention.
neurips-2025-moba-mixture-of-block-atten.tldr: MoBA applies mixture-of-experts principles to attention, enabling model-directed sparsity and transitions between sparse and full attention.

paragraphs: Does reinforcement learning teach new reasoning strategies, or mainly make an existing model produce its better answers more often? ProRL investigates this question through prolonged training. Its methodology combines control of KL divergence, resetting the reference policy, and a diverse collection of tasks to support extended reinforcement learning.

The authors compare trained and base models across pass-at-k evaluations, which examine success when multiple attempts are allowed. The trained models consistently perform better, including on cases where base models fail throughout extensive sampling. These observations support the paper's argument that prolonged reinforcement learning can uncover strategies unavailable to the base models in the tested sampling conditions.

The extent of improvement is strongly correlated with the base model's competence on a task and with training duration. The authors interpret this as evidence that reinforcement learning can gradually explore additional regions of the solution space. The findings identify circumstances in which extended training meaningfully broadens observed reasoning capability, rather than establishing that additional reinforcement-learning compute always produces the same benefit.
neurips-2025-prorl-prolonged-reinforceme.tldr: ProRL provides empirical evidence that prolonged reinforcement learning can uncover reasoning strategies beyond those found by extensive base-model sampling.

paragraphs: AI work is often called rigorous when its mathematical, statistical, or computational methods are applied correctly. This position paper argues that this understanding is too narrow. The authors contend that it has contributed to concerns raised in responsible AI, including claims about system capabilities that go beyond what the evidence supports.

Their proposed framework includes six dimensions. Methodological rigor concerns methods themselves. Epistemic rigor examines the background knowledge informing what researchers choose to study. Normative rigor addresses the influence of standards, beliefs, and community expectations. Conceptual rigor asks whether the theoretical ideas used in the work are clearly articulated.

The remaining dimensions concern communication and inference: reporting rigor addresses what is reported and how, while interpretative rigor asks whether conclusions are adequately supported by available evidence. Together, these dimensions offer a vocabulary for examining AI research and practice more broadly. The paper presents this as a framework for dialogue among researchers, policymakers, journalists, and other stakeholders, extending scrutiny from technical execution to the choices and interpretations surrounding it.
neurips-2025-rigor-in-ai-doing-rigorous-.tldr: This position paper proposes six dimensions of rigor spanning methods, background knowledge, norms, concepts, reporting, and interpretation.

paragraphs: Understanding a video stream requires a model to keep updating its answers as events unfold. RTV-Bench evaluates this continuous process rather than only isolated video judgments. Its questions can have different answers at different timestamps, making changes in the scene part of what the model must track.

The benchmark combines basic and advanced questions and evaluates perception, understanding, and reasoning separately. It contains 552 videos totaling 167.2 hours and 4,631 question-answer pairs. The evaluation covers proprietary models, open-source models designed for offline video processing, and open-source models designed for real-time interaction, enabling comparisons across these different approaches.

In the reported results, open-source real-time models generally outperform their offline counterparts but remain behind the strongest proprietary models. Increasing model size or frame sampling rates does not significantly improve performance and sometimes slightly reduces it. These findings motivate architectures better suited to streams and long sequences. The benchmark makes sustained updating of video understanding an explicit evaluation target, rather than assuming it follows from strong performance on other multimodal tasks.
neurips-2025-rtv-bench-benchmarking-mllm.tldr: RTV-Bench tests whether multimodal models continuously update their understanding and answers as video scenes change.

paragraphs: This paper studies how tightly learning theory can bound excess risk as the number of training examples increases. Its starting point is algorithmic stability, an approach used to connect a learning procedure with its generalization behavior. Earlier stability-based analysis for strongly convex learners gives high-probability bounds of order log(n)/n.

The authors analyze sharper rates under assumptions on the loss: the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition, smoothness, and Lipschitz continuity. They report that rates of order log²(n)/n² are achievable under these conditions. The distinction concerns the dependence of the bound on sample size: the denominator grows quadratically, accompanied by a squared logarithmic factor.

The paper also presents what the authors describe, to their knowledge, as the tightest high-probability bounds for gradient-based generalization gaps in nonconvex settings. The contribution is therefore a theoretical refinement of what stability analysis can establish. Its meaning depends on the stated loss assumptions: it provides sharper conditional guarantees about learning behavior, rather than an empirical claim that every trained model will exhibit this rate.
neurips-2025-stability-and-sharper-risk-.tldr: Under stated loss assumptions, the paper derives sharper stability-based risk bounds with a log²(n)/n² rate.

paragraphs: Removing unsafe behavior from an image generator may not keep that behavior suppressed after subsequent customization. This paper finds that existing safety-driven unlearning methods can largely lose their effectiveness even when downstream fine-tuning uses entirely benign data. ResAlign is designed to make the initial unlearning step more resilient to those later changes.

The framework incorporates downstream fine-tuning into an implicit optimization problem. A Moreau-envelope reformulation enables efficient gradient estimation, allowing the unlearning process to target the later recovery of harmful behavior. A meta-learning strategy also simulates a varied distribution of fine-tuning scenarios so that resilience is trained across different possible adaptations.

Experiments span multiple datasets, fine-tuning methods, and configurations. ResAlign consistently retains safety better than prior unlearning approaches in these evaluations while preserving benign image-generation capability. The findings highlight the importance of evaluating unlearning after further training, not only immediately after removal. They also support anticipating downstream optimization during unlearning as a practical way to reduce the return of unwanted behaviors.
neurips-2025-towards-resilient-safety-dr.tldr: ResAlign trains safety-driven unlearning to better withstand later diffusion-model fine-tuning, including customization on benign data.

paragraphs: Training models to understand hour-long videos requires suitable long-video examples as well as an architecture that can process them. This paper addresses both needs with VideoMarathon and Hour-LLaVA. VideoMarathon contains around 9,700 hours of videos, with individual recordings lasting between three and 60 minutes, accompanied by 3.3 million question-answer pairs.

The dataset covers temporal and spatial information, objects, actions, scenes, and events. Its 22 tasks require both short-term and long-term comprehension. Hour-LLaVA builds on this resource with a memory augmentation module that draws from cached information about the full video. The module adaptively integrates content relevant to the question and informative about space and time.

This design supports hour-long training and inference while sampling one frame per second. The authors report the best performance on multiple representative long-video language benchmarks in their experiments. The combined contribution links extended training coverage with a way to selectively use a video's stored context, supporting questions whose useful evidence may be spread across a long recording.
neurips-2025-unleashing-hour-scale-video.tldr: VideoMarathon and Hour-LLaVA combine long-video supervision with adaptive memory to support hour-scale video understanding.

paragraphs: Unlearnable examples protect data by adding imperceptible perturbations intended to interfere with unauthorized training. Existing approaches often produce perturbations tied closely to a particular training set, losing effectiveness on new data or tasks. This paper studies transfer across changes in visual style, classes outside the training distribution, image resolution, and model architecture.

Its Versatile Transferable Generator uses two mechanisms to address these changes. Adversarial Domain Augmentation synthesizes out-of-distribution examples during training, exposing the generator to unfamiliar conditions. Perturbation-Label Coupling uses contrastive learning to align perturbations directly with class labels, reducing reliance on the semantic content of the original examples.

Together, these mechanisms aim to make protective perturbations less dependent on a particular data distribution. Extensive experiments support the generator's effectiveness and broad applicability across the studied settings. The contribution concerns transferability as much as protection on an original training set: a reusable generator must continue to disrupt learning when the data conditions or learning architecture change. The reported results support that objective across the evaluated variations.
neurips-2025-versatile-transferable-unle.tldr: VTG generates protective data perturbations designed to remain effective across changes in style, classes, resolution, and learning architecture.
